p01-stream-title.name: p01-stream-title
p01-stream-title.text: With no distribution we can only go one sample at a time: each time one arrives, adjust the weight a bit

p01-stream-ctx.name: p01-stream-ctx
p01-stream-ctx.text: One dimension: the target is $y\approx w^{\ast}x$ and the learner does not know $w^{\ast}$. The lecture demo's first two samples: $(0.692,\,1.047)$ and $(0.928,\,1.711)$. Learning rate $\rho=0.08$, start $w_0=0$.

p01-stream-src.name: p01-stream-src
p01-stream-src.text: Source: KP08 lecture §4 first two samples and $w_1,w_2$ (table numbers); the true value $w^{\ast}=1.8$ is the lecture demo's setting, invisible to the learner, and the dashed line is only for the reader's comparison.

p01-stream-c0.name: p01-stream-c0
p01-stream-c0.text: Without the full data distribution we cannot use KP07's closed-form solution. Instead: each time a sample $(x_k,y_k)$ is read, correct once with the current error. See the first two samples.

p01-stream-c1.name: p01-stream-c1
p01-stream-c1.text: Sample 1 $(0.692,\,1.047)$. The current line $w_0=0$ predicts $0$, error $e_1=1.047$ (orange dashed): far off.

p01-stream-c2.name: p01-stream-c2
p01-stream-c2.text: One correction: $w_1=0.058$. The line tilts up slightly (green line).

p01-stream-c3.name: p01-stream-c3
p01-stream-c3.text: Sample 2 $(0.928,\,1.711)$. The line now predicts $0.054$, error $e_2=1.657$, still large.

p01-stream-c4.name: p01-stream-c4
p01-stream-c4.text: Correct again: $w_2=0.181$, the line tilts up again (dark green line). Each sample moves it only a little, so it takes many samples to approach $1.8$. This "one sample replaces the expectation" approach is LMS.

p02-update-title.name: p02-update-title
p02-update-title.text: One LMS step: predict with the old weight, compute the error, then correct

p02-update-ctx.name: p02-update-ctx
p02-update-ctx.text: $\widehat y_k=x_kw_{k-1}$  $e_k=y_k-\widehat y_k$  $w_k=w_{k-1}+\rho\,x_k\,e_k$. The prediction always uses the weight "before the update".

p02-update-src.name: p02-update-src
p02-update-src.text: Source: KP08 lecture §2: replace the expectation in the MSE gradient $-2E[\mathbf xe]$ by the single quantity $\mathbf x_ke_k$, the constant 2 absorbed into $\rho$; numbers from sample 1 of the lecture §4 table.

p02-update-c0.name: p02-update-c0
p02-update-c0.text: Five boxes from left to right. Sample 1: $x_1=0.692$, $y_1=1.047$. What number goes in each box?

p02-update-c5.name: p02-update-c5
p02-update-c5.text: Why correct this way? KP07's MSE gradient is $-2E[\mathbf x\,e]$ and we go opposite to it. The expectation cannot be computed, so use the current sample's $x_ke_k$ as an estimate (the constant 2 absorbed into $\rho$). The order cannot be reversed: if we updated first and predicted afterwards, the error would no longer be the "error before correction".

p03-signs-title.name: p03-signs-title
p03-signs-title.text: Which way does the correction go? Look at the sign of the feature times the sign of the error

p03-signs-ctx.name: p03-signs-ctx
p03-signs-ctx.text: Correction $\rho\,x\,e$. Take $\rho=0.1$ and compute each of the four cases. We cannot just say "the error is positive, so every weight goes up".

p03-signs-src.name: p03-signs-src
p03-signs-src.text: Source: KP08 lecture §2: the sign of the correction depends on both residual and feature; a negative feature reverses it. The four numbers are a teaching example ($x=\pm2$, $e=\pm1$).

p03-signs-c0.name: p03-signs-c0
p03-signs-c0.text: Four combinations: the feature $x$ and the error $e$ each positive or negative. What is the direction of the correction $\rho x e$? First guess which two go up and which two go down.

p03-signs-c1.name: p03-signs-c1
p03-signs-c1.text: Product positive (same sign): up. $x$ and $e$ both positive, or both negative.

p03-signs-c2.name: p03-signs-c2
p03-signs-c2.text: Product negative (opposite signs): down. With a negative feature the correction goes opposite to the error.

p03-signs-c3.name: p03-signs-c3
p03-signs-c3.text: Whether the weight grows or shrinks is decided by the sign of the product of $x$ and $e$, not by the error alone.

p04-mean-title.name: p04-mean-title
p04-mean-title.text: The simplest warm-up: the same form can also compute the mean one sample at a time

p04-mean-ctx.name: p04-mean-ctx
p04-mean-ctx.text: General form $w_k=w_{k-1}+\rho_kF(x_k,w_{k-1})$. Take $F=x_k-w$ and $\rho_k=1/k$: each time reweight the old mean and the new reading.

p04-mean-src.name: p04-mean-src
p04-mean-src.text: Source: KP08 lecture §3 [supplement]: with readings $2,4,3$ the estimates are $2,3,3$; this is only a warm-up for stochastic approximation, not a claim that every LMS problem reduces to averaging.

p04-mean-c0.name: p04-mean-c0
p04-mean-c0.text: The readings come in as $2,\,4,\,3$. After each one, what does the estimate $w_k$ become? Is it the same as "the average so far"?

p04-mean-c4.name: p04-mean-c4
p04-mean-c4.text: The three estimates $2,3,3$ are exactly "the average so far" $2,\,(2+4)/2,\,(2+4+3)/3$. The benefit of per-sample updating: no need to store all readings. But this is a special case; we cannot treat every LMS problem as averaging.

p05-paths-title.name: p05-paths-title
p05-paths-title.text: The same data, three fixed step sizes: how does the weight move? Does every step improve?

p05-paths-ctx.name: p05-paths-ctx
p05-paths-ctx.text: This page uses the 260 samples simulated in this task ($y=1.8x+$ noise, noise standard deviation $0.28$, seed $20261108$). Three fixed step sizes $\rho=0.005,0.08,0.25$.

p05-paths-src.name: p05-paths-src
p05-paths-src.text: Source: The lecture demo's 260 samples use the source's own random function (not provided), so they cannot be reproduced; this plot simulates the same setting with NumPy. The lecture's end values 1.2768, 1.8064, 1.7931 are not this plot's numbers.

p05-paths-c0.name: p05-paths-c0
p05-paths-c0.text: How will each of the three step sizes go? Is bigger better? Does every step get closer to the true value?

p05-paths-c1.name: p05-paths-c1
p05-paths-c1.text: $\rho=0.005$: too small, after 260 samples it reaches only $1.242$, still far off.

p05-paths-c3.name: p05-paths-c3
p05-paths-c3.text: $\rho=0.25$: fastest at first but also jitters most, ending at $1.782$.

p05-paths-c4.name: p05-paths-c4
p05-paths-c4.text: In the $260$ steps of $\rho=0.08$, $117$ steps moved the estimate further from $1.8$. Each step uses one noisy sample, so not every step improves; and this is only one sample path, which cannot rank step sizes by end values nor prove convergence.

p06-stability-title.name: p06-stability-title
p06-stability-title.text: How small must the step be for stability? Mean stability and mean-square stability are two different thresholds

p06-stability-ctx.name: p06-stability-ctx
p06-stability-ctx.text: Scalar, no noise, inputs independent standard Gaussian ($R=E[x^2]=1$). Look at the multiplier of "how many times the error shrinks" each step. Below 1 it converges.

p06-stability-src.name: p06-stability-src
p06-stability-src.text: Source: KP08 lecture §5: mean stability $0<\rho<2/\lambda_{\max}(R_x)$; [supplement] mean-square multiplier $1-2\rho+3\rho^2$ needs $0<\rho<2/3$; series conditions need data assumptions.

p06-stability-onet.name: p06-stability-onet
p06-stability-onet.text: 1: only below it does it shrink

p06-stability-c0.name: p06-stability-c0
p06-stability-c0.text: Which curve corresponds to each of the two kinds of "stability"? Are their upper limits the same? Convergence needs the red dashed 1 to be above the curve.

p06-stability-c1.name: p06-stability-c1
p06-stability-c1.text: Blue: the multiplier of the "mean", $|1-\rho|$: $E[w_k-w^{\ast}]$ is multiplied by it each step. Below 1 needs $0<\rho<2$ (the blue point is at $\rho=2$).

p06-stability-c2.name: p06-stability-c2
p06-stability-c2.text: Red: the "mean-square" multiplier $1-2\rho+3\rho^2$ (involving the fourth moment). Below 1 needs only $0<\rho<2/3$: much smaller than the mean's limit of 2.

p06-stability-c3.name: p06-stability-c3
p06-stability-c3.text: So: mean stability is not mean-square stability. The step must account for both; the series condition $\sum\rho_k=\infty,\sum\rho_k^2<\infty$ (e.g. $1/k$) guarantees convergence only under assumptions such as stable data and informative features. A fixed small step keeps jittering but can also track a slowly changing target.

p07-adaline-title.name: p07-adaline-title
p07-adaline-title.text: LMS (Adaline) versus the perceptron: for a correctly classified point, LMS may still update

p07-adaline-ctx.name: p07-adaline-ctx
p07-adaline-ctx.text: The same sample $x=1$, target $y=+1$, current $w=0.2$. Compare whether the two rules update and by how much.

p07-adaline-src.name: p07-adaline-src
p07-adaline-src.text: Source: KP08 lecture §6: perceptron corrects on classification failure, LMS on continuous error, so a correct sample can still update. $w=0.2,x=1,y=1,\rho=0.5$ is a teaching example.

p07-adaline-c0.name: p07-adaline-c0
p07-adaline-c0.text: Output $\widehat y=xw=0.2$, positive, the same sign as the target $+1$: the classification is correct. What does each rule do?

p07-adaline-al_t.name: p07-adaline-al_t
p07-adaline-al_t.text: LMS: look at the error $e=y-\widehat y$

p07-adaline-c2.name: p07-adaline-c2
p07-adaline-c2.text: $e=1-0.2=0.8\ne0$: still far from the target, update: $w=0.2+0.5(1)(0.8)=0.6$.

p07-adaline-c3.name: p07-adaline-c3
p07-adaline-c3.text: The perceptron only asks "is it correct?" and does nothing if so; LMS asks "how far from the target", so a correct point still pushes $w$ toward the target as long as the output has not reached about $\pm1$. Conversely, it also pulls back when the output "overshoots" the target.

p07-adaline-c4.name: p07-adaline-c4
p07-adaline-c4.text: Computation and storage per sample grow with the number of features $d$. When feature scales differ a lot, updates may be fast and slow by turns; implementations should check scales, finiteness and the error trajectory (lecture "going deeper").

p08-practice-title.name: p08-practice-title
p08-practice-title.text: Practice: w=0.4, ρ=0.1, x=2, y=1.5: prediction, residual, new weight

p08-practice-ctx.name: p08-practice-ctx
p08-practice-ctx.text: Work it out first. Hint: the prediction uses the weight before the update; the residual is target minus prediction, not the target itself. Press Next when done.

p08-practice-src.name: p08-practice-src
p08-practice-src.text: Source: KP08 lecture practice; answer computed by build_kp08_en.py and recomputed independently by check_numbers_kp08.py.

p08-practice-q.name: p08-practice-q
p08-practice-q.text: (a) The prediction $\widehat y$? (b) The residual $e$? (c) The new weight? (d) Is the prediction under the new weight closer to the target $1.5$?

p08-practice-a4.name: p08-practice-a4
p08-practice-a4.text: (d) Yes. The prediction under the new weight is $2\times0.54=1.08$, closer to the target $1.5$ (the error falls from $0.7$ to $0.42$).

p09-summary-title.name: p09-summary-title
p09-summary-title.text: Summary: with no distribution, correct step by step with the error of one sample at a time

p09-summary-ctx.name: p09-summary-ctx
p09-summary-ctx.text: Recall the corrections of the first two samples; the five conclusions of this KP are on the right.

p09-summary-e0.name: p09-summary-e0
p09-summary-e0.text: No distribution: LMS uses one sample's $x_ke_k$ in place of the expectation in the MSE gradient

p09-summary-e1.name: p09-summary-e1
p09-summary-e1.text: One step: $\widehat y=xw_{k-1}$, $e=y-\widehat y$, $w_k=w_{k-1}+\rho xe$; the prediction uses the old weight; the direction is set by the sign of the product of $x$ and $e$

p09-summary-e2.name: p09-summary-e2
p09-summary-e2.text: Each step uses one noisy sample: not necessarily an improvement; a fixed step jitters, a decreasing step is steadier but tracks change less well

p09-summary-e3.name: p09-summary-e3
p09-summary-e3.text: Mean stability ($\rho<2/\lambda_{\max}$) ≠ mean-square stability (here $\rho<2/3$); series conditions need data assumptions

p09-summary-e4.name: p09-summary-e4
p09-summary-e4.text: Open question: when the whole finite data set is at hand we need not approximate one by one but can solve least squares directly. Next KP: least squares and the pseudoinverse
